title: Synaptic depth from the photoreceptors did not predict slower or more low-pass flicker responses in 39 fly visual cell types (FlyWire and male CNS connectomes)
abstract: Question: does a fly visual cell type that is more synaptic steps from the photoreceptors have a slower, more low-pass response? Campaign tests of this temporal-hierarchy idea were null at region level in mouse cortex and larval zebrafish. The fly optic lobe gives wiring and activity at cell-type resolution. Data: full-field flicker calcium responses (0.1 to 2 Hz, trial means; Currier and Clandinin 2025, CC0) of 39 types, 299 cells and 58 flies; depth from a probabilistic traversal from all photoreceptors in FlyWire v783 and male CNS v1.0. We froze the plan before we computed any depth. Result: depth did not predict the low-pass index log2(A0.5Hz/A2Hz): FlyWire rho -0.05, one-sided permutation p 0.62, fly-bootstrap 95% interval -0.20 to 0.24; male CNS rho -0.23. Depth also did not predict group delay, sustainedness or across-fly consistency (Holm p 0.40 to 0.89). Hop count, right-side depth, other indices and type subsets gave no positive result. Power for a true rank correlation of 0.4 was 0.80. Limitations: anatomy and activity come from different flies; most types lie at 2.5 to 3.1 steps; trial means at 5 Hz sampling; one stimulus.

Mouse cortex: anatomical hierarchy did not reliably predict timescales; we add a cell-type-level null in the fly.
Larval zebrafish: projectome hierarchy did not predict timescales; same direction of evidence.
